stages.title: High-fidelity aerospace CFD
stages.hook: Direct simulation of every eddy around a full airliner would need more grid points than all computers on Earth can store. So which parts of turbulence do we resolve, and which do we model?
explain: Turbulence spans a range of scales. The largest eddies are of the size of the body, while the smallest (the Kolmogorov scale) are set by viscosity and dissipation rate: η = (ν³ ÷ ε)^¼. Direct numerical simulation (DNS) resolves all scales, and its cost grows roughly as Re^(9/4) in grid points, which is out of reach at flight Reynolds numbers of 10⁷ to 10⁸. Large-eddy simulation (LES) resolves large eddies and models small ones; RANS models all of the turbulence; hybrid RANS-LES (such as detached-eddy simulation) uses RANS near walls and LES in separated regions.

Numerical quality matters as much as the physical model. A scheme of order p has truncation error that scales as h^p; Richardson extrapolation estimates the grid-converged value from two meshes with refinement ratio r: f_exact ≈ f₁ + (f₁ − f₂) ÷ (r^p − 1), where f₁ is the fine-grid solution. Low-dissipation schemes are needed for LES, shock-capturing schemes for transonic flow, and unstructured or overset grids for complex geometry. Adjoint methods give sensitivities of lift or drag to thousands of shape variables for design.

Credibility requires uncertainty quantification: errors from the mesh, the turbulence model, boundary conditions and the experiment itself. Standard cases such as the NASA Common Research Model in the Drag Prediction Workshops have shown scatter between codes of the order of tens of drag counts (one count is C_D = 0.0001), far larger than the design gains sought. Machine learning is being tested to correct RANS models, but physical consistency and generalisation are active research issues.

example.q: Kolmogorov length: ν = 1.46×10⁻⁵ m²/s and dissipation rate ε = 1 m²/s³. Find η. Then estimate how the number of DNS grid points changes when Re rises from 10⁶ to 10⁷.
example.a: η ≈ 0.24 mm; grid points rise about 178 times

misc.wrong: Higher-fidelity simulation (LES or DNS) is always better than RANS for design.

stages.limits: Scaling laws such as Re^(9/4) are estimates for homogeneous turbulence. Wall-modelled LES reduces the cost for wall-bounded flows, and the scaling is then closer to Re^1 to Re^1.3.

questions.q: Why can an adjoint method make aerodynamic shape optimisation practical with thousands of design variables?

questions.why: Adjoint cost scales with the number of objectives and constraints, not design variables.

panel.q: If the Kolmogorov scale is 0.24 mm and the body is 6 m long, roughly how many grid cells would be needed along each direction to resolve η with 1 cell per η?

About 25
About 250

panel.q: Why is validation against high-quality experimental data still necessary when CFD is highly refined?
panel.model: A numerically converged solution can still have modelling error, such as an inadequate turbulence or transition model. Only comparison against reliable measurements, with their own uncertainties, shows whether the simulated physics is right.
panel.why: Verification does not establish physical correctness.

teach.topic: Why we cannot simulate every eddy
teach.model: Turbulence has eddies from body size down to tiny dissipation scales, and resolving them all costs far too much at flight Reynolds numbers. LES resolves the big eddies and models the small, and RANS models all of it. Engineers choose the fidelity that fits the question and always check numerical and model error.

stages.title: Hypersonic flow and aerothermodynamics
stages.hook: A re-entering capsule is surrounded by glowing plasma hotter than the surface of the Sun on an ideal-gas estimate, yet its heat shield survives. What really sets the heating?
explain: Hypersonic flow (above about Mach 5) has strong shocks close to the body, high temperatures behind them and thin shock layers. The stagnation enthalpy per unit mass is h₀ = h + V²/2; for an ideal gas the stagnation temperature is T₀ = T + V²/(2c_p). At V = 7500 m/s with T = 220 K and c_p = 1005 J/(kg·K), the ideal-gas value is about 28 000 K, which is not what occurs. At those energies the air dissociates (O₂ → 2O, N₂ → 2N) and ionises, absorbing energy, so the real gas temperature is much lower, thousands of kelvin. The ideal-gas γ = 1.4 is not valid, so equilibrium or non-equilibrium chemistry models are needed.

A normal shock in an ideal gas has a density ratio ρ₂/ρ₁ = (γ+1)M²/((γ−1)M²+2), with limit (γ+1)/(γ−1) = 6 as M → ∞; real-gas effects increase it. In Newtonian theory the pressure coefficient on a surface inclined at angle θ to the flow is C_p = 2 sin²θ, a useful first estimate of hypersonic pressure loads. At high Mach numbers, force coefficients become nearly independent of Mach number (Mach number independence).

Heating is estimated with correlations such as Sutton-Graves: q̇ = k √(ρ/R_n) V³, with k = 1.7415×10⁻⁴ (SI units, for Earth air), where R_n is the nose radius. A blunt body has a lower heat flux because a large R_n means a smaller q̇ and a detached bow shock. Thermal protection systems include ablative materials (PICA, carbon-phenolic), reusable tiles and cooled structures. Hypersonic air-breathing propulsion (scramjets) is limited by mixing and combustion in milliseconds.

example.q: Sutton-Graves: find the stagnation-point convective heat flux for V = 7500 m/s, ρ = 1.0×10⁻⁴ kg/m³ and nose radius R_n = 1 m (k = 1.7415×10⁻⁴).

panel.q: Why can't wind-tunnel tests alone reproduce true hypersonic flight conditions?
panel.model: Ground facilities struggle to match both the high total enthalpy and the full size of the vehicle, and tests last milliseconds, so real-gas chemistry may not fully develop. Results are combined with CFD and flight data.
panel.why: No single facility reproduces all hypersonic parameters.

teach.topic: Why re-entry heating is dominated by blunt shapes and real-gas effects
teach.model: At hypersonic speed a strong shock heats the air so much that molecules break apart, which soaks up energy. A blunt body pushes the shock away from the surface and sends most of the heat into the air. Heat flux grows as speed cubed, so heat shields ablate or insulate to survive.

stages.title: Nonlinear flight dynamics
stages.hook: Linear stability theory predicts that a stable aircraft recovers from small disturbances. Why do real aircraft still stall, spin, or roll out of control when pushed hard?
explain: The six-degree-of-freedom rigid-body equations of motion are nonlinear: m(u̇ + qw − rv) = X, with similar equations for the other axes, and Euler's equations such as I_x ṗ − (I_y − I_z) q r = L for principal axes (ignoring I_xz). Terms like qr are products of angular rates, so a rolling aircraft couples pitch and yaw motion (inertia coupling). Linearising about a trim state gives modes (phugoid, short period, Dutch roll, spiral, roll) that are valid for small perturbations.

Large-amplitude phenomena need nonlinear analysis: stall hysteresis, wing rock, spin, pitch-up and departure, and control saturation. Aerodynamic coefficients vary nonlinearly with angle of attack and sideslip, and separated flow is unsteady. Bifurcation analysis follows how equilibria and oscillations appear or vanish as a parameter (like angle of attack or control deflection) changes; the aircraft can jump between states (e.g. from trimmed flight to a flat spin).

In a steady level turn with load factor n, the turn rate is ω = g√(n² − 1) ÷ V, and the bank angle is φ = arccos(1/n). Structural limits and maximum lift C_Lmax bound n. Lyapunov methods and numerical continuation give stability regions; flight control laws use gain scheduling, nonlinear dynamic inversion and envelope protection to keep the aircraft within the recoverable region.

example.q: A fighter turns at V = 200 m/s with load factor n = 4. Find the turn rate in degrees per second (g = 9.81 m/s²).

analogies.sport: A bicycle that wobbles slightly recovers, but a big wobble becomes a fall.
analogies.sea: A small boat in small waves rights itself; in a very large wave it can capsize (a nonlinear threshold).
analogies.music: A guitar string plucked lightly vibrates cleanly, but plucked hard changes pitch because of nonlinearity.
analogies.nature: A ball at the top of a hill with two valleys: nudged lightly it returns, nudged hard it falls into another valley.

misc.right: Linear stability only guarantees local recovery. Large disturbances or control saturation can leave the region of attraction, so the aircraft may enter a stall, spin or other departure.

stages.limits: Rigid-body models ignore flexibility and engine gyroscopics. Aerodynamic models for high angles of attack are uncertain, and flight test is needed to validate them. The game is educational, not pilot training.

stages.title: Advanced aeroelasticity
stages.hook: A fighter loaded with stores can start a steady oscillation of its wings even though no individual part is faulty. How do engineers predict such behaviour, and what changes at transonic speeds?
explain: Flutter analysis couples structural dynamics, M q̈ + K q = Q_aero, with unsteady aerodynamics. Theodorsen's function C(k) accounts for the lag between wing motion and lift in incompressible oscillating flow, where the reduced frequency is k = ωb ÷ V (b = semi-chord). Methods such as the p-k and g methods solve an eigenproblem for each speed to find where a mode's damping crosses zero. Finite element structures are combined with doublet-lattice aerodynamics in subsonic flow, and CFD-based reduced-order models are used in transonic flow.

The transonic flutter 'dip' is a drop in flutter speed near Mach 0.8 to 1.0, caused by shock motion on the wing. Nonlinearities such as structural free-play, control-surface backlash and separated flow produce limit-cycle oscillations (LCO), where the amplitude saturates instead of growing without bound. Aeroservoelasticity (ASE) couples structural modes with the flight control system: sensors can feed structural vibration back into control commands, and notch filters or gain-stabilisation are used to prevent such interaction.

Gust loads are another area. For a discrete gust, the load factor increment can be estimated as Δn = ρ U_de V_e a K_g ÷ (2 (W/S)), where U_de is the derived gust velocity, V_e equivalent airspeed, a the lift-curve slope per radian, K_g the gust alleviation factor and W/S the wing loading. Active gust load alleviation uses control surfaces to reduce loads. Certification combines analysis with ground vibration and flight flutter testing.

example.q: A wing has W/S = 3000 N/m², a = 5 per rad, K_g = 0.8, flying at V_e = 150 m/s through a derived gust U_de = 15.2 m/s (ρ = 1.225 kg/m³). Find Δn.
steps: Numerator = ρ U_de V_e a K_g = 1.225 × 15.2 × 150 × 5 × 0.8.

teach.topic: How flutter is predicted and why transonic and nonlinear effects matter
teach.model: Engineers build a structural model with natural frequencies and add unsteady aerodynamics, then look for the speed at which a mode's damping reaches zero. stages.title: Integrated aircraft design
stages.hook: Wing size, engine thrust, fuel and weight depend on each other: a bigger wing adds weight, which needs more thrust, which needs more fuel, which adds weight. How does a designer break this circle?
explain: Conceptual design is iterative. Take-off gross weight W₀ is the sum of crew, payload, fuel and empty weight. With fuel fraction W_f/W₀ and empty fraction W_e/W₀ from statistics or sizing, W₀ = (W_crew + W_payload) ÷ (1 − W_f/W₀ − W_e/W₀). Because W_e/W₀ itself depends on W₀, the equation is solved by iteration until it converges.

The constraint diagram plots thrust-to-weight T/W against wing loading W/S for requirements such as stall speed, take-off distance, climb gradient, cruise and manoeuvre. The stall condition gives W/S ≤ ½ρV_s²C_Lmax. The design point is chosen in the feasible region, usually at the minimum T/W. For a parabolic polar C_D = C_D0 + k C_L², maximum L/D = 1/(2√(C_D0 k)) at C_L = √(C_D0/k).

Decisions also involve cost, noise, emissions, manufacturability, maintainability, certification and safety. Trade studies use weighted decision matrices or multidisciplinary design optimisation. Risk is managed with a failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA): risk = likelihood × severity. Emerging concepts, such as hybrid-electric aircraft, boundary-layer ingestion and hydrogen propulsion, change the weight, volume and drag models, so existing statistical relations may no longer apply.

stages.title: Advanced rotorcraft engineering
stages.hook: Why have helicopters, which can hover, never flown as fast as aeroplanes, and what are tilt-rotors and compound helicopters doing about it?
explain: Blade element momentum theory (BEMT) combines blade-element lift on each section with momentum theory for the induced inflow. For an untwisted, rectangular blade in hover with uniform inflow ratio λ, the thrust coefficient is C_T = (σ a ÷ 2)(θ₀/3 − λ/2), where σ is solidity, a the section lift-curve slope and θ₀ the pitch. Momentum theory gives λ = √(C_T/2); the two must be solved consistently. Twisted blades make the loading more uniform.

Forward flight limits come from the advancing-blade tip Mach number, M_tip = (ΩR + V)/a, and retreating-blade stall and reverse flow. The rotor is a periodic system: blade flapping about a hinge with offset e has frequency ratio ω_β/Ω ≈ √(1 + 3e/(2(1 − e))). A rotor with N_b blades transmits vibration at N_b per revolution to the fuselage: a 4-bladed rotor at 5 Hz produces 20 Hz vibration. Blade-vortex interaction (BVI) causes impulsive noise in descent.

To fly faster, designs separate lift from propulsion: tilt-rotors (rotors tilt from vertical to horizontal) and compound helicopters (add wings and propellers). Each has trade-offs: higher disk loading in a tilt-rotor lowers hover efficiency, and the addition of wings adds download in hover and mass. Rotor dynamics also include aeromechanical stability (ground and air resonance), whirl flutter in tilt-rotors, and active vibration control. Electric VTOL aircraft use distributed propulsion, with trade-offs in battery energy density.

example.q: A rotor has σ = 0.085, a = 5.7, θ₀ = 0.12 rad and uniform inflow ratio λ = 0.05. Find the thrust coefficient (untwisted blade).

stages.title: Space mission optimisation
stages.hook: Launch windows to Mars open only about every two years, and a good transfer can cut propellant by tons. How do mission designers find the best trajectory?
explain: A mission is designed around its Δv budget and constraints. Interplanetary transfers use the patched-conic method: a heliocentric Hohmann ellipse between planets, then a hyperbolic escape from Earth. For Earth to Mars (1 to 1.524 AU), the heliocentric transfer needs a perihelion speed 32.73 km/s versus Earth's 29.78 km/s, so the hyperbolic excess speed is v∞ ≈ 2.95 km/s. From a 400 km circular parking orbit the departure burn is Δv = √(v∞² + 2μ/r) − √(μ/r) ≈ 3.57 km/s, and the trip takes about 259 days. Launch opportunities repeat at the synodic period 1/|1/T₁ − 1/T₂| ≈ 780 days.

Lambert's problem finds the orbit connecting two positions in a given time; solving it over a grid of departure and arrival dates gives a porkchop plot of C₃ = v∞² or Δv. Gravity assists change a spacecraft's heliocentric velocity at no propellant cost by using a planet's motion. The Oberth effect means a burn is most effective at high speed, deep in a gravity well. Low-thrust electric propulsion has high Isp but low thrust, so trajectories spiral, and optimal control methods (direct collocation) compute them.

Mission optimisation is multi-objective: Δv, flight time, payload mass, cost, risk and planetary protection. Typical practice is to add margin (for example 5 to 10% on Δv and 20 to 30% mass margin early on) and to maintain contingency. System-level trades cover launcher selection, staging, propulsion type and operations, all of which interact through the rocket equation.

stages.title: Entry, descent and landing
stages.hook: Landing on Mars needs a heat shield, a parachute and a rocket, while landing on the Moon needs only rockets. What does the atmosphere change?
explain: Entry, descent and landing (EDL) removes the orbital kinetic energy of a spacecraft in minutes. In a ballistic entry, the vehicle's deceleration depends on the ballistic coefficient β = m ÷ (C_D A). For a steep ballistic entry in an exponential atmosphere with scale height H, the Allen-Eggers solution gives the peak deceleration a_max = V_E² sin γ_E ÷ (2 e H), independent of β, where V_E is entry speed, γ_E the entry flight-path angle (magnitude) and e = 2.718. For Earth, H ≈ 7.2 km: with V_E = 7800 m/s and γ_E = 5° this is about 135 m/s², or 13.8 g.

Entry vehicles can be steered by lift: a capsule with an offset centre of mass flies at a trim angle of attack and rolls to direct its lift vector, giving a lifting entry with peak decelerations of order 3 to 4 g and some landing-site control. A shallow angle skips; too steep means high g and heating, so there is an entry corridor. Heating peaks earlier in entry than the peak deceleration. Heat shields use ablative or reusable materials.

After hypersonic flight, parachutes slow the vehicle to the terminal velocity v_t = √(2mg ÷ (ρ C_D A)). On Mars the air is about 1% as dense as at Earth's surface, so parachutes cannot slow a heavy lander enough, and the final landing uses retrorockets, a sky crane or airbags. On airless bodies such as the Moon the entire descent uses propulsion. Landing accuracy depends on navigation, hazard detection and terrain-relative sensing.

stages.title: Integrated aircraft or spacecraft mission project
stages.hook: Pick a mission: a solar-powered aircraft that stays aloft for weeks, or a spacecraft that visits another planet. How do the pieces you have studied combine into one design that closes?
explain: A project starts with requirements and a concept of operations, then moves through system sizing, analysis, trade studies, verification and risk management. Systems engineering turns objectives into requirements, allocates them to subsystems, tracks interfaces and budgets (mass, power, Δv, link, thermal), and verifies each requirement by test, analysis, inspection or demonstration. Margins are kept at each stage and reduced as the design matures.

Example: a high-altitude solar UAV of mass 150 kg flying at 20 m/s with L/D = 25. Level flight needs drag power P = W V ÷ (L/D) = 1471.5 × 20 ÷ 25 = 1177 W at the wing. With a propulsive chain efficiency of 0.70 the electrical power is 1682 W. A 12-hour night needs 1682 × 12 = 20.2 kWh from batteries; at 250 Wh/kg that is 80.7 kg, more than half of the aircraft's mass. The loop shows the key challenge: energy storage mass drives the design. Raising L/D, lowering mass, or choosing a lower latitude and season changes the result.

For a spacecraft, the same discipline combines the rocket equation, orbit design, power and thermal balance, attitude control, communications and EDL. Decisions use weighted matrices, sensitivity analysis and Monte Carlo analysis of margins. Reliability and safety analysis (FMEA, fault trees) and verification (tests such as vibration, thermal vacuum) support readiness reviews. Ethical and societal matters count too: space debris, planetary protection, noise and emissions, and equitable access to the benefits.

misc.wrong: If each subsystem meets its own requirements, the whole system must work.
misc.right: Interfaces and interactions can cause failures even if each part meets specification, so integrated testing and system-level analysis are essential.

stages.limits: The examples here are simplified. Real projects need detailed models, test data, regulation, and expert review. The game is educational, not a substitute for professional engineering or pilot training.

trip.prompt: Find the V-model diagram. Which steps check that the final product meets the original requirements?

questions.q: A 150 kg UAV (g = 9.81 m/s²) flies at 20 m/s with L/D = 25. What is the drag power P = W V/(L/D) in watts?
With an efficiency of 0.70, what electrical power does it need (1177 W at the wing)? Answer in watts.
The UAV needs 1681.5 W for a 12 h night. Battery specific energy is 250 Wh/kg. What battery mass is needed in kg?
What does a mass budget do?
o: Tracks the mass of each subsystem against an allocation and margin
Sets the ticket prices for the flight
Counts the passengers on board only
Measures the drag on the airframe
questions.why: Mass budgets keep the design within the vehicle's limit.

questions.q: The UAV's battery is over half of the aircraft's mass. Which change helps the design most?
o: Raising L/D or battery specific energy
Painting the whole airframe white
Adding more passengers for balance
Reducing the wing area to nearly zero
questions.why: Lower power demand or lighter storage reduces battery mass.

questions.q: Why are interfaces a major source of failures?
o: Parts that work alone can be incompatible when combined
Interfaces have no physics, so they cannot fail
They always work if each part passes its own test
They are cheap and so need no attention
questions.why: Mismatched assumptions at boundaries cause many failures.

questions.q: Why does a long-endurance solar aircraft fly slowly at high L/D?
o: Power required is proportional to W V/(L/D), so low speed and high L/D reduce power
Solar cells need time to charge, so it must go slowly
It cannot go any faster than the walking pace of a person
Slow flight is more exciting for the pilot
questions.why: Minimising required power reduces the energy to store.

questions.q: Which statement best describes a margin?
o: A reserve held to cover uncertainty and growth
Waste that should be removed from the design
A rule that bans testing near the end
The last page of the final report
questions.why: Margins protect the design against unknowns.

questions.q: Put these project steps in order.
items: Define requirements and concept of operations
Size the design and perform trade studies
questions.why: Systems engineering moves from needs to design to verification.

questions.q: A student's mission design closes only because every margin was set to zero. Explain what is wrong and what should be done.
questions.model: A design with no margin has no protection against uncertainties and mass or performance growth, so small errors would make the mission fail. The student should restore appropriate margins, then re-size or adjust the design to close with them.
questions.why: Margins are part of the requirement.

panel.q: If battery specific energy rises from 250 to 400 Wh/kg, the battery mass for the same night energy (20 178 Wh) becomes about
o: 50 kg
81 kg
126 kg
20 kg

panel.q: A trade matrix scores Concept A 80 and Concept B 78. Sensitivity analysis shows A's rank changes if the weight on cost rises by 10%. What do you conclude?
o: The choice is not robust; consider the decision further
A is always best, because it has the higher score
B is always best, because the weights can change
Scores do not matter, so the choice can be made freely
panel.why: Sensitivity checks whether the decision holds under reasonable changes.

panel.q: Name two ethical or societal considerations in a space or aviation project and say why they matter.
panel.model: Space debris can make orbits unusable and endanger other spacecraft, and aviation emissions and noise affect climate and communities. Considering these protects people and the environment and keeps space and air travel sustainable for everyone.
panel.why: Engineering decisions have consequences beyond the mission.

teach.topic: How an integrated mission design is closed
teach.model: A mission starts with clear requirements. Engineers estimate the power, mass and Δv needed, size the subsystems, and check that budgets close with margins. Trade studies compare options, and testing and review show the design meets its requirements.

points.ask: Where does the design start?
How do the numbers fit together?
What protects against unknowns?
How do you know it works?
